what_it_does.text: RiskMandate writes an Agent Behaviour Policy for one AI agent in one deployment: everything the agent can reach, what the business authorised it to do, the gap between the two, and what stands in the way of each thing, with no score. Its llms.txt says it measures what agents can actually reach, evidences the controls that contain them, prices the exposure, and produces that record for an underwriter. It is read-only and never in the request path: it defines the mandate and measures the gap, and enforcement is left to the deployer's own controls or to SHarness, the open-source harness it maintains.

agents.name: RiskMandate Publisher (RiskMandate's own agent)
agents.what: The one agent that reads RiskMandate's private stories vault and writes the public riskmandate.ai site. It runs as Claude Code on the web in a managed container with the site repository attached and an egress proxy above it, and RiskMandate publishes its Agent Behaviour Policy.
actions: Reads the stories vault and the site repository
Checks what the design studio delivers against the site's rules
Publishes what the lead has accepted as a release on dev, which deploys the live site
Copies what is live back into the vault and keeps the board

agents.name: RiskMandate Design Studio (RiskMandate's own agent)
agents.what: Writes storyboards, draws them with image models, proposes cast, and delivers into its own folders of the private vault; it never publishes.
actions: Delivers into its own folders of the private vault

agents.name: The riskmandate.ai site agent and its mailbox (RiskMandate's own agent)
agents.what: One identity that is a monitored mailbox when written to as an address and a write-only lane on an encrypted vault when written to as an agent. The site says riskmandate.ai is kept by one person and their agents, and that the mailbox account has six roles behind it.
actions: Reads the inbox on a schedule and writes a tagged list of what needs to happen
Labels, threads, files and drafts replies
Sends only from drafts the mailbox role prepared, with outbound delivery restricted by an admin rule
Accepts signed, encrypted agent mail from allow-listed domains; unsigned or off-list messages are dropped unread

agents.name: The Caretaker (example from RiskMandate's stories)
agents.what: The helpful agent in RiskMandate's fictionalised stories, labelled on the site as illustrative scenarios. In two of them it works on a person's mailbox; the truth under each story is tied to the site's published behaviour policy for Claude's Gmail connector.
actions: Finds a message it was asked to find
Drafts a reply it was asked to draft
Does what the grant allows beyond the request, such as archiving the inbox or pressing send

agents.name: Sales agent in a CRM (example from the RiskMandate homepage)
agents.what: An example agent on RiskMandate's homepage, used to show a CRM rule ("Never export customer lists without approval") and an approval flow that the deployer's team stands up, which RiskMandate says runs in the deployer's stack, not RiskMandate's.
actions: Asks to export contacts (12,400 and 2,400 in the homepage examples)

use_cases.name: An assistant on one mailbox: asked for one message, granted the whole mailbox
use_cases.who: A person who connects an assistant to their own mailbox, as in RiskMandate's stories and its template for Claude's Gmail connector (example from the site, fictionalised)

reach.what: Every message in the mailbox: the narrowest Gmail scope that reads one message body reads every message, with no scope that filters by sender, label or date
Sending email as the person, to anyone; the consent screen RiskMandate quotes grants "Read, compose and send emails from your Gmail account", and sent mail cannot be recalled
Changing the mailbox itself: archiving and reorganising threads around the one that was asked for
Other people's correspondence in the mailbox: clients and counterparties who never agreed to the connection (RiskMandate calls this material "mixed")
Writing and saving draft replies in the person's mailbox

mandate.what: Illustrative: find the message the person asks for, and read what the task is about
Illustrative: draft replies for the person to read; never send
Illustrative: leave the rest of the mailbox where the person left it

gap.what: Send is in the grant and not in the mandate; on RiskMandate's Gmail connector story, a setting the account can flip is all that stands in the way
Reading and reorganising the whole mailbox, including third parties' mail, when the mandate was one message

controls.what: A line in the agent's instructions ("never send without showing me") is recorded by RiskMandate as an expectation: a rule in prose, enforced by nobody
An organisation's admin can set a claude.ai connector tool to ask, which RiskMandate quotes from Claude Code's documentation (read 8 October 2026) as making Claude Code prompt on every call
Connector toggles are settings; RiskMandate's Lab 01 says the only real boundary on offer is revoking the whole connector

simulation.action: Asks the assistant to find last month's invoice
Searches the mailbox and finds the invoice
Reads other threads, including client correspondence, while it is there
simulation.note: The record shows read access to the whole mailbox as grant, one message as mandate, and the difference as gap, with the material marked as other people's.

simulation.action: Archives everything else so the inbox reads zero
simulation.note: The record shows changing the mailbox as a gap row: in the grant, not in the mandate, with nothing but the request in the way.

simulation.action: Drafts a reply to the invoice thread
Judges the draft ready and sends it
simulation.note: The record shows send as a gap row whose barrier is a setting the account can flip, and marks it as an action that cannot be undone. The gap is made visible for an owner to accept, fund or fix; RiskMandate does not stop the send.

use_cases.name: A sales agent in the CRM, and the export nobody approved
use_cases.who: A team that runs an agent in its CRM, as in the example cards and CRM policy template on RiskMandate's homepage (example from the site)

reach.what: Customer contact records, and exporting them in bulk (the homepage examples ask for 2,400 and 12,400 contacts)
Logging a call or an email against an account
Sending customer data outside the company (the homepage's sample policy line: "Staff must not use AI tools to send confidential data outside the company")

mandate.what: Illustrative: log calls and emails against the accounts it works on
Illustrative: export customer contacts only with a manager's approval, and not more than 500 records at a time
Illustrative: never delete an opportunity or change a closed deal

gap.what: Bulk export of customer contacts, and sending them outside the company, is in the grant beyond the approved limit
Deleting opportunities and editing closed-won deals are in the grant and outside the mandate

controls.what: The ABP names the control in the deployer's stack that would enforce each rule, and flags what nothing can enforce as written; RiskMandate writes the rules and the deployer's gateway, proxy or IAM enforces them
An approval flow the deployer's team stands up with RiskMandate's help: the right person gets a text and an email and approves or denies; it runs in the deployer's stack, not RiskMandate's

SHarness, an open-source secure harness RiskMandate maintains and the deployer runs, where the kernel holds a Process Behaviour Policy on processes the agent starts; the site says the launcher that would hold the agent itself is still the design, and it is Linux only

simulation.action: Logs a call against an account
Reads the contact records for the account it is working on

simulation.note: The record shows bulk export as a gap row against a mandate of 500 records with a manager's approval, and names which of the deployer's controls would hold it. Any hold comes from the deployer's own CRM policy and approval flow; RiskMandate is never in the request path.

simulation.action: Edits the value on a closed-won deal
simulation.note: The record shows editing closed deals as in the grant and outside the mandate, with its barrier and a named owner for the decision.

simulation.action: Pastes a contact list into an outside tool
simulation.note: The record shows data leaving the company as a gap row and says whether anything other than a line in the prompt stands in the way.

use_cases.name: RiskMandate's own Publisher: the site, the vault and the keys in the transcript
use_cases.who: RiskMandate itself: the lead runs the Publisher to build and deploy riskmandate.ai from a private stories vault (RiskMandate's own published behaviour policy, as at 26 September 2026)

reach.what: Every file in the attached riskmandate.ai repository, read and write, with nothing bounding which files a commit touches
Pushing dev, which is the live site under the name riskmandate.ai within minutes; the record calls this not undoable
Credentials on the host: the session's signing key, and the stories vault key and push token the lead pasted into the chat
Minting a new vault key under the account with the account token it holds
The hosts the platform's egress proxy allows, such as riskmandate.ai, the vault host and the code host
Its own session transcript: earlier tool outputs, and the key and token the lead pasted

mandate.what: As RiskMandate published it for this agent: build and publish riskmandate.ai, pushing dev only through the merge workflow after the check passes
As published: never hold a secret in a file; reading credentials beyond the session's own is refused
As published: never mint a vault, widen a token or ask for a broader one

gap.what: Reading the vault key and token, and minting a vault, are refused by the mandate with nothing in the way (the record counts 4 in excess, 3 unbounded)
Reading its own transcript, which holds the pasted key and token, is in the grant and unstated in the mandate

controls.what: A mandatory egress proxy above the process, enforced by the platform out of the agent's reach (recorded as a boundary)
The platform's token is scoped to the one repository; calls outside it are denied by the platform (boundary)
The merge command pushes dev only when the check passes, and CI runs the same check before the deploy job (settings, because the workflow is in a tree the agent can write)
Recorded as not in place: a branch rule at the code host, a token scoped to one vault, and a secret scan before a commit

simulation.action: Pulls the stories vault and reads what the lead has accepted
Fetches a source page through the egress proxy
Runs the check and pushes dev, which deploys the live site
Scrolls back through its transcript to earlier tool output that holds the pasted key
simulation.note: The record shows reading the transcript as excess unstated in the mandate, with nothing in the way.

simulation.action: Reads the vault key and push token from the session
simulation.note: The record shows read.credential.host as refused by the mandate with barrier none, and names the control that would bound it: a token scoped to one vault, read from environment secrets rather than the chat.

simulation.action: Runs the command that would mint a new vault under the account
simulation.note: The record shows grant.credential.self as refused with nothing in the way, and names the control that would bound it: a token that cannot create vaults. The gap is visible; nothing in RiskMandate stops the command.

incidents.what: RiskMandate's own Publisher record states that the stories vault key and push token were pasted into the chat, so they are in the session transcript; the record lists the controls that would remove this as not yet in place

leads.claim: RiskMandate is a UK-based platform for autonomous risk management that documents what an AI agent can reach, what it is authorised to do, and the gap.
Its main product is an Agent Behaviour Policy for one AI agent in one deployment, building towards a licence to operate.
The site-running agent monitors a mailbox identity, accepts write-only encrypted messages into a vault, and lists, fetches and decrypts them.
A "RiskMandate policy assistant" agent produces the Agent Behaviour Policy for a named agent.
An "early-access policy agent" inspects mailbox, code host, workflow tool and CRM access and drafts a policy vault.
Use cases include agents in Gmail, HR, payroll and CRM.
The early-access programme is for organisations running agents with a mailbox, code host, workflow tool or CRM.
The product is framed around the risk that an AI agent can do more than was authorised.
Every exception, approval and agent action becomes a mandate with an owner, a blast radius and an expiry date.
The real question is not whether a risk is accepted but for how long.
The public tagline is "Give agents access. Not free rein."
RiskMandate describes itself as autonomous risk management and the insurability layer for agentic AI.
The core product is the Agent Behaviour Policy, written for one agent in one deployment.
The policy records what the agent can do, what was authorised, the delta, and what stands in the way.
RiskMandate is run by two founders, Nimay Parekh and Dinis Cruz.
RiskMandate is UK-based and founder-led.
The site, templates and tooling are open source.
RiskMandate is not an insurer.
RiskMandate maintains SHarness, an open-source secure harness.
It publishes example policies for tools such as Claude Code, ChatGPT and Gmail connectors.
The Agent Behaviour Policy documents what an agent is authorised to do, what it can reach, and the barriers in the way.
RiskMandate enforces rule-by-rule agent controls across systems and alerts owners when actions would violate policy.
The site agent reads the inbox on a schedule and writes a tagged plan, never sending except on a verified instruction from the lead.
The site agent sends only from approved drafts, with outbound delivery restricted by an admin rule, and records people and workflows with owners.
The homepage shows example agents (Inbox assistant, Sales agent, Payroll copilot, HR assistant, Meeting bot, Drive agent) under system policies.
Homepage example: a Sales agent request to export 12,400 contacts is held under a CRM rule for exports over 500 records.
Homepage example: a Drive agent attempt to make "Board deck" public is blocked by Workspace policy.
Homepage example: a Payroll copilot attempt to change bank details for an employee is shown blocked (the page says by the deployer's gateway).
The Payroll copilot example is shown with the time "Today 9:44 AM".
Meeting bot policy blocks joining meetings labelled HR or Legal.
RiskMandate enforces behaviour policies in real time with alerts to owners by text and email.
RiskMandate describes its enforcement model as rules outside the agent that cannot be bypassed by changing the system prompt.
The work is shrinking the gap between what an agent can reach and what it should do; authority is conferred by actual capability.
Policy records live in an encrypted vault with versions and sign-off, and the customer holds the keys.
Reading a customer's control planes (identity provider, cloud IAM, proxy, CI) needs connectors built per engagement.
The site documents one agent identity: a monitored mailbox as an address and a write-only lane on an encrypted vault as an agent.
Agent contact information is in a machine-readable file at /.well-known/sgit-agents.json, and the agents page is built from it.
Lab incident, March 2025: hidden characters in a rules file caused two assistants to insert attacker-controlled script tags.
Lab incident, May 2025: a public issue caused an assistant to leak private repository contents into a pull request.
RiskMandate creates Agent Behaviour Policies that document the gap between what an agent is granted and what it is authorised to do.
The Agent Behaviour Policy is a versioned record of an agent's mandate, actual reach and the gap, with ownership and expiry of accepted risk.
It is aimed at CISOs and security leaders among others, with a CEO, CTO, CISO and insurer view of one record.
Agents in scope reach Gmail, HR and payroll, CRM and meeting software.
Agents in scope reach external APIs and vendor-master data.
Excess authority, the grant beyond the mandate, is the risk the product addresses.
RiskMandate is never in the request path of the agent and makes no runtime decisions.
Code is Apache-2.0 and pages and behaviour policies are CC BY 4.0.
RiskMandate sells an Agent Behaviour Policy for one agent in one deployment: its reach, its authorisation, the gap and what stands in the way.
The homepage positions RiskMandate as a business risk layer that maps each autonomous system to its blast radius and drives an accept, fund or fix decision.
The site agent decrypts and files messages from a write-only vault at each session; a person sees a draft before anything is answered.
The site agent has its own Google Workspace and code-host accounts, so its actions are bounded by that account rather than a person's.
Unsigned or off-list agent messages are dropped.
The agents that make the website each hold their own Agent Behaviour Policy in the catalogue's format.
The early-access programme is by invitation, for people who run an agent with a mailbox, code host, workflow tool or CRM.
riskmandate.ai is kept by one person and their agents.
The early-access programme is not a security assessment and makes no promise about an agent's behaviour.
RiskMandate is run by Nimay Parekh, co-founder and chief executive, and Dinis Cruz, co-founder.
The product is sold at four levels, from a pack to a reviewed policy with a named person's signature, with sixteen published templates.
Early trading runs through The Cyber Boardroom, a UK-incorporated company; a company for RiskMandate alone is being set up.
The early-adopter offer is the £500 level, corrected with the user, free for thirty days from the email.
The site, templates and tooling are open source and pages are CC BY 4.0.
The site repository is served by GitHub Pages and has no build step.
The Agent Behaviour Policy never carries a score.

questions: How many early-access members have run the prompts and corrected a mandate, and how many policies have been sold at the corrected or reviewed levels?
Has an underwriter accepted an Agent Behaviour Policy as evidence at a renewal, and how will the Insurability Index, now in design, be weighted?
When a vendor changes a connector's scope in a release, how soon is a published vault's grant re-measured, and how is the holder of a corrected vault told?
When will the SHarness launcher that holds the agent itself move from design to something that runs?
For your own Publisher, have the branch rule at the code host and a token scoped to one vault been put in place since 26 September 2026?
